overview: Micron Technology designs, manufactures, and sells memory and storage semiconductors — DRAM, NAND flash, and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) — serving data center, PC, mobile, automotive, and industrial customers worldwide. Headquartered in Boise, Idaho, Micron is one of only three vertically integrated DRAM makers globally (alongside Samsung and SK Hynix) and competes in NAND against Samsung, SK Hynix/Solidigm, Kioxia, and SanDisk/Western Digital. The company is currently riding an unprecedented AI-driven memory supercycle, with fiscal 2026 revenue of $133.2 billion, up from $37.4 billion in fiscal 2025.

business_model.summary: Micron manufactures commodity and specialty memory chips (DRAM, NAND, HBM) and sells them to OEMs, cloud/data-center operators, and through retail channels (Crucial brand). Revenue is highly cyclical and price-sensitive to industry-wide supply/demand balance; the business is capital- and R&D-intensive, requiring leading-edge process nodes (1-gamma DRAM, G9 NAND) and multi-year fab construction cycles. Historically a boom-bust commodity business, the AI buildout has shifted mix sharply toward higher-margin, contracted data-center and HBM products.
business_model.customer_type: B2B — hyperscale cloud/AI datacenter operators, OEMs (smartphone, PC, auto, industrial), with a smaller B2C retail channel (Crucial)
business_model.geographic_mix: Manufacturing concentrated in the US (Idaho, Virginia), Taiwan, Japan, and Singapore; sales global with historically meaningful but declining China/Asia exposure after Micron exited China's server/critical-infrastructure market in 2023-2025 following Beijing's restrictions

competitive_position.market_position: Micron is the #2-3 global DRAM supplier (~25% share in Q2 2026, narrowing the gap with Samsung's ~39% and overtaking a weakened SK Hynix in some quarters) and a growing #3 NAND supplier (~15% share, behind Samsung ~28% and SK Hynix ~19%). In HBM, Micron is a fast-rising but still smaller player (roughly 5-20% share) behind SK Hynix (50-62%) and Samsung (25-40%), having been the surprise share-gainer of the current cycle with HBM4 volume shipments for NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform.

moat_factors.factor: Oligopoly structure / high barriers to entry
moat_factors.description: DRAM and advanced NAND require tens of billions in capex and multi-year process R&D; only three scaled DRAM makers exist globally, limiting new entrants
1-gamma DRAM node and HBM4/HBM4E roadmap keep Micron competitive on performance/bit-density, though SK Hynix and Samsung often lead on bleeding-edge HBM timing
Micron's entire calendar 2026 HBM supply is under price-and-volume agreements with customers, providing revenue visibility atypical for a commodity business
Up to $6.1B in direct CHIPS Act funding for Idaho and New York fabs lowers the cost of US capacity expansion and provides geopolitical insulation
In-house wafer fabrication, packaging, and test across DRAM/NAND/HBM supports cost position versus fabless or less-integrated peers

weaknesses: Commodity product with limited pricing power outside of supply-constrained up-cycles; historically brutal down-cycle margin collapses
Smaller HBM share than SK Hynix and Samsung, the two leaders in the fastest-growing, highest-margin memory category
Effectively locked out of the China server/critical-infrastructure market since 2023-2025, ceding share to Samsung, SK Hynix, and domestic Chinese suppliers (CXMT, YMTC)
High fixed-cost, high-capex manufacturing model makes margins extremely sensitive to utilization and industry-wide bit-supply growth
Heavy ongoing capex (guided above $25B in FY2026) could pressure free cash flow in a demand pullback

growth_drivers: AI/datacenter-driven HBM demand — management forecasts the HBM TAM growing from ~$35B in 2025 to ~$100B by 2028, pulled forward two years by AI accelerator demand

Data center DRAM and NAND content growth — data center DRAM/NAND bit shipments in calendar 2026 expected to more than double versus two years prior, with AI/server TAM exceeding 50% of industry TAM for the first time
HBM4/HBM4E product ramp — HBM4 36GB 12H volume shipments for NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform began in Q1 calendar 2026; HBM4E in development with 1-gamma node for calendar 2027 ramp
Capacity expansion — new/expanded fabs in Idaho (first wafer output mid-2027), New York (groundbreaking January 2026, up to four fabs over 20+ years), Taiwan (Tongluo), Japan, Singapore, and India
CHIPS Act subsidies (~$6.1B) lowering the cost of US capacity buildout and supporting domestic supply chain resilience narrative
Structural supply tightness — management has signaled industry supply will stay tight through fiscal 2027-2028, supporting sustained pricing and margin strength
Data center SSD and enterprise storage growth — data center SSD revenue nearly 10x year-over-year in fiscal Q4 2026

business.description: DRAM/NAND pricing is historically volatile with multi-year boom-bust cycles; the current AI-driven upcycle could reverse sharply if hyperscaler capex slows or supply floods the market
SK Hynix and Samsung hold larger shares of the highest-growth, highest-margin HBM segment; losing design wins on next-gen HBM4E/HBM5 could cap Micron's upside
A growing share of revenue is tied to a handful of hyperscale/AI customers (e.g., NVIDIA platform cycles), increasing sensitivity to any single customer's capex pullback

financial.description: FY2026 capex guided above $25B; sustained heavy investment could pressure free cash flow if pricing normalizes before new capacity is amortized
Q4 FY2026 adjusted gross margin of 87% is far above historical norms and could compress quickly in a supply-demand rebalancing

regulatory.description: Escalating and shifting US export control regimes on AI-related semiconductors (and China's retaliatory measures, including China's 2023 ban on Micron products in critical infrastructure) create ongoing uncertainty over addressable market and compliance costs

Micron has effectively exited China's server/critical-infrastructure market, ceding share to competitors and Chinese domestic suppliers (CXMT, YMTC), which also benefit from Beijing's industrial policy support
Direct federal funding agreements carry conditions (e.g., profit-sharing above certain return thresholds, restrictions on buybacks/China expansion) that could constrain capital allocation flexibility

macro.description: A substantial portion of current growth is tied to hyperscaler AI infrastructure spending; any slowdown in AI data center buildouts would directly hit DRAM/HBM demand and pricing

macro.risk: Global economic slowdown / PC and smartphone demand
macro.description: Non-AI end markets (PC, mobile, auto) remain cyclical and sensitive to consumer and enterprise IT spending
Significant international manufacturing (Taiwan, Japan, Singapore) exposes Micron to currency fluctuations and equipment/raw material cost swings

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Memory industry is in a historic AI-driven upcycle; data center DRAM/NAND demand expected to more than double over two years, with HBM TAM projected to nearly triple from ~$35B (2025) to ~$100B (2028)
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — memory is one of the most cyclical semiconductor sub-sectors, with pricing driven by industry-wide bit-supply growth versus demand; current conditions are the tightest/most favorable in over a decade
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — high capex intensity and project financing needs make the business sensitive to borrowing costs, though current net cash position and strong FCF reduce near-term sensitivity
key_input_costs: Semiconductor fab equipment (lithography, deposition, etch tools)
Skilled fab labor and engineering talent

recent_developments.event: Reported record fiscal Q4 2026 results: revenue of $54.23B (up 379% YoY) and adjusted EPS of $33.42, beating analyst estimates; adjusted gross margin reached 87.0%
Issued Q1 FY2027 guidance of $61.5B ± $1.5B revenue and adjusted EPS of $38.15 ± $1.00, both above consensus, with gross margin guided at 86.25%
Full fiscal year 2026 revenue reached $133.19B (vs. $37.38B in FY2025) with adjusted net income of $86.76B ($75.52/share)
Multiple analysts raised price targets following earnings (DA Davidson to $2,100, Rosenblatt to $1,900, Cantor Fitzgerald maintained $2,000), citing supply tightness extending through FY2027-2028

Stock crossed $1,000/share for the first time, fueling speculation about a stock split (none announced as of October 2026); Micron's Canadian Depositary Receipts completed a 5-for-1 split in March 2026
Broke ground on first New York fab (Clay, NY); plan includes up to four fabs over 20+ years, with supply expected from 2030 onward
Began HBM4 36GB 12H volume shipments for NVIDIA's Vera Rubin AI platform
Reallocated CHIPS Act funding to accelerate a second Idaho fab, with New York fabs proceeding on a longer timeline
Industry data confirms Micron narrowing the DRAM share gap with Samsung/SK Hynix and gaining HBM allocation share faster than expected, per Counterpoint Research and other industry trackers

items.notes: Above consensus of ~$57.0B; implies continued sequential growth driven by AI/data-center demand and tight supply
Above consensus of ~$35.14; reflects sustained pricing strength
Slightly below Q4 FY2026's 87.0% actual but still near record levels, reflecting continued supply-constrained pricing
Funding expansion across Taiwan (Tongluo), Idaho, New York, Japan, Singapore, and India to meet long-term AI-driven demand
Management pulled forward its TAM forecast by two years given accelerating AI accelerator demand; entire CY2026 HBM supply already under price/volume agreements

guidance.management_commentary: Management signaled that industry-wide memory supply will remain tight through fiscal 2027-2028, supporting continued pricing power and margin strength. Leadership emphasized HBM4 volume ramp for NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform and HBM4E development on the 1-gamma node as key differentiators, alongside record contributions from data center DRAM and SSD products. Despite a heightened capex outlook, shares dipped briefly after the print before recovering as analysts framed increased capex as a response to demand that outstrips even Micron's aggressive capacity plans.

bull_case: Historic AI-driven memory supercycle with HBM TAM forecast to nearly triple (~$35B to ~$100B) by 2028, and Micron gaining share faster than expected against SK Hynix and Samsung
Record profitability (87% adjusted gross margin, $86.8B adjusted net income in FY2026) with management guidance signaling supply stays tight through FY2027-2028
Full CY2026 HBM supply already locked in under price-and-volume agreements, providing unusual revenue visibility for a historically commodity business
US-based capacity expansion (Idaho, New York) backed by ~$6.1B in CHIPS Act funding reduces geopolitical and supply-chain risk versus Asia-concentrated peers
Broad-based Wall Street bullishness (zero sell ratings, numerous price target increases post-Q4 earnings) reflects conviction the up-cycle has durable legs
bear_case: Memory is a deeply cyclical commodity business; current 87% gross margins and record profitability are historically unsustainable and vulnerable to sharp reversion if AI capex growth decelerates or supply catches up with demand

Micron remains the smallest of the three scaled HBM suppliers behind SK Hynix and Samsung, risking share loss on next-generation HBM4E/HBM5 design wins in the most strategically important memory category
Heavy ongoing capex (>$25B guided for FY2026) across multiple new fabs increases execution risk and could strain free cash flow if the pricing environment normalizes before new capacity is absorbed

Escalating and unpredictable US-China export control policy, plus Micron's effective exclusion from China's server/critical-infrastructure market, creates ongoing geopolitical and addressable-market risk

Valuation prices in sustained supercycle conditions (stock up ~720% over the past year); any disappointment relative to extremely high guidance bars (Q1 FY2027 EPS of ~$38) could trigger a sharp correction
